summary: Valdecoxib (formerly marketed as Bextra) was a selective COX-2 inhibitor NSAID approved for osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, and primary dysmenorrhoea. It was WITHDRAWN from the US and EU markets in 2005 because of an unfavourable risk-benefit profile: an increased risk of serious cardiovascular events and life-threatening skin reactions (Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis), with no demonstrated advantage over other NSAIDs. It is no longer FDA-approved or marketed; this record is provided for historical/reference and safety awareness only.

moa: Valdecoxib selectively inhibits cyclo-oxygenase-2 (COX-2), the inducible enzyme responsible for prostaglandin synthesis at sites of inflammation, thereby reducing pain and inflammation while largely sparing COX-1-mediated gastric mucosal and platelet prostaglandins. The COX-2 selectivity that was intended to reduce gastrointestinal toxicity is also linked to a prothrombotic imbalance contributing to cardiovascular risk.

preg: Avoid in pregnancy, particularly the third trimester, as NSAIDs may cause premature closure of the ductus arteriosus and impair fetal renal function. (Moot — the drug is withdrawn.)
lact: NSAIDs are excreted in breast milk; avoid during breastfeeding. (Moot — the drug is withdrawn.)
renal: Avoid in significant renal impairment; NSAIDs can cause sodium/fluid retention and acute kidney injury. (Moot — withdrawn.)
hepatic: Avoid in moderate-to-severe hepatic impairment. (Moot — withdrawn.)

major: Other NSAIDs / aspirin — additive GI bleeding and ulceration risk
Antihypertensives (ACE inhibitors, ARBs, diuretics) — reduced effect and renal risk

CYP2C9 substrates/inhibitors (valdecoxib metabolised partly by CYP2C9 and CYP3A4)

overdose: There is limited overdose experience. NSAID overdose may cause drowsiness, nausea, vomiting, epigastric pain, GI bleeding, and, less commonly, renal impairment, hypertension, respiratory depression, or seizures. Management is supportive with gastric decontamination if early; there is no specific antidote, and the drug is highly protein-bound (dialysis of limited value).
